log.why: E9 tests three genes with roughly 50% combined prior probability, maximally splitting the hypothesis space.
E4 (10 µM) splits Ticket 2's prior probability mass most evenly (0.437 vs 0.563) while Ticket 1 incubates.
Test the leading candidate ftsZ directly; a positive result strongly confirms it, while a negative result narrows the culprit to gyrA or ompF.
Testing at 30 µM splits the remaining probability mass evenly between 30 µM and higher thresholds.
Ticket 1 is most urgent and knocking out gyrA directly distinguishes between the two remaining likely candidates, gyrA and ompF.
Treat at 100 µM (E6) to decisively distinguish between the 100 µM (0.562) and 300 µM (0.349) threshold hypotheses.
Ticket 1 has only 30s left and ompF is at 0.586; E3 directly tests ompF to confirm before publishing.
Posterior for 100 5M is strong at 0.815 after both 30 5M and 100 5M boundary tests.
Ticket 1 is uninformative and expiring; bisect Ticket 3's prior using E10 to test {trpE, dnaK, rpoB} with 0.531 probability.
E7 tests gyrA and trpE, which cross-cuts the growing E10 plate to uniquely identify all four leading candidate genes before Ticket 3 expires.
Ticket 3 will expire before a paper can finish; E5 on Ticket 4 splits the probability mass best by testing top candidates recA and hisG.
Crossing E9 {recA, trpE, katG} with growing E5 {recA, hisG} cleanly separates recA, hisG, metJ, and katG before Ticket 4 expires.
Both E5 and E9 lost the phenotype, pointing strongly to their common gene recA with 0.894 posterior, and time is expiring.
E3 (3 µM) splits Ticket 6's prior mass nearly in half (0.529 vs 0.471), maximizing information gain with 25s left in the round.
With 19s left in the round, running E4 alongside growing E3 on Ticket 6 distinguishes 3, 10, and 30 µM in time to publish.
Only 1 second remains in the round, so no publish or experiment can complete in time.
